children.text: tatra nirvartako heturiti lakṣaṇāt yo hi yasya nirvartako bījabhāvenāvasthitaḥ sa tasya hetupratyayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, because of the definition 'a cause is that which brings about,' whatever, being present in the condition of a seed, brings about a given thing is its cause-condition (<s>hetupratyaya</s>), indeed.
The object-support by means of which a dharma arises while arising is its object-condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>), indeed.
The immediately preceding cessation of the cause is the condition for the arising of the effect.
For example, the immediately preceding cessation of the seed is the condition for the sprout's arising.

children.text: yasmin sati yadbhavati tattasyādhipateyamiti ta ete catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ ||
children.translated_text: When that exists, this comes to be; that is its dominant condition. Thus these are the four conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>).
And the others, such as those born before, born together, and born afterward, are included in these very conditions.
But things such as <s>Īśvara</s> are not possible as conditions at all.

children.text: ata evāvadhārayati pratyayo nāsti pañcama iti ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason he states the restriction: there is no fifth condition.
Therefore, since there is production of entities from these, which are other than them, there is production from another.

children.text: atrocyate naiva hi bhāvānāṃ parabhūtebhyaḥ pratyayebhya utpattiriti ||
children.translated_text: To this it is replied: entities are certainly not produced from conditions that are other than them.
Because:

children.text: yadi hi hetvādiṣu parabhūteṣu pratyayeṣu samasteṣu vyasteṣu vyastasamasteṣu hetupratyayasāmagryā anyatra vā kvacid bhāvānāṃ kāryāṇāmutpādātpūrvaṃ sattvaṃ syāt syāttebhya utpādaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For if entities, as effects, existed before their production in cause and the other conditions, which are other than them, whether taken collectively, separately, separately and collectively, in the complex of cause-conditions, or somewhere else, then production from them would be possible.
But it is not so that there is such an existence before production.

children.text: yadi syād gṛhyeta cotpādavaiyarthyaṃ ca syāt ||
children.translated_text: If there were, it would be apprehended, and production would also be pointless.
Therefore the own-being (<s>svabhāva</s>) of entities does not exist in the conditions beginning with the condition.
And when own-being is absent, there is no other-being.
Becoming is being; it is arising.
Arising from others is other-being.
That does not exist.
Therefore this is untenable: that entities are produced from things other than them.

children.text: athavā bhāvānāṃ kāryāṇām aṅkurādīnāṃ bījādiṣu pratyayeṣu satsvavikṛtarūpeṣu nāsti svabhāvo nirhetukatvaprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: Alternatively, if the conditions such as seed exist in an unaltered form, then entities, the effects such as sprouts, have no own-being in those seed and other conditions, because the unacceptable consequence would follow that they are without cause.
Then with reference to what would conditions and the like be other?
For only when two things exist, such as <s>Maitra</s> and <s>Upagrāhaka</s>, is their otherness relative to one another.
But seed and sprout are not simultaneous in that way.

children.text: tasmādavidyamāne svabhāve kāryāṇāṃ parabhāvaḥ paratvaṃ bījādīnāṃ nāstīti paravyapadeśābhāvādeva na parata utpāda iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the own-being of effects is absent, the other-being, that is, the otherness of seed and the rest, does not exist; and precisely because there is no designation as 'other,' there is no production from another.
Therefore the opponent is certainly ignorant of the intention of scripture.
For <s>Tathāgatas</s> do not utter a statement that is contrary to reason.
And the intention of scripture has already been explained before.

children.text: tadevaṃ pratyayebhya utpādavādini pratiṣiddhe kriyāta utpādavādī manyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, when the proponent of production from conditions has been refuted, the proponent of production from activity thinks:
The conditions, such as eye and form, do not directly produce consciousness.
Rather, because they accomplish the activity that produces consciousness, they are called conditions.
And that activity produces consciousness.

children.text: tasmāt pratyayavatī vijñānajanikriyā vijñānajanikā na pratyayāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore an activity producing consciousness, possessed of conditions, is what produces consciousness, not the conditions themselves.
Just as the preparatory cooking activity produces cooked rice.
It is replied:

children.text: yadi kriyā kācit syātsā cakṣurādibhiḥ pratyayaiḥ pratyayavatī vijñānaṃ janayet ||
children.translated_text: If there were some activity, then, being possessed of conditions such as the eye, it would produce consciousness.
But there is none.

children.text: kathaṃ kṛtvā iha kriyeyamiṣyamāṇā jāte vā vijñāna iṣyate ajāte vā jāyamāne vā ||
children.translated_text: How so? Here, if this activity is accepted, is it accepted when consciousness has already arisen, when it has not yet arisen, or when it is arising?

children.text: tatra jāte na yuktā kriyā hi bhāvaniṣpādakā bhāvaścenniṣpannaḥ kimasya kriyayā
children.translated_text: In that case, when it has already arisen, activity is not reasonable; for activity accomplishes an entity, and if the entity has been accomplished, what use is its activity?

children.text: jātasya janma punareva ca naiva yuktam
children.translated_text: And birth again of what has already been born is certainly not reasonable.
This has been established in the <s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> by words such as these.
Nor is it reasonable when it has not yet arisen.

children.text: kartrā vinā janiriyaṃ na ca yuktarūpā ||
children.translated_text: This birth without an agent is not of a reasonable form.
Because of statements such as this.

children.text: jāyamāne'pi bhāve kriyā na saṃbhavati jātājātavyatirekeṇa jāyamānābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is activity possible when the entity is arising, because apart from the born and the unborn there is no 'arising' thing.
As has been said:
Because the arising thing would be half-born, the arising thing is not born;
or else the state of being arising would apply to absolutely everything.
Thus.

children.text: yataścaivaṃ triṣu kāleṣu janikriyāyā asaṃbhavastasmānnāsti sā ||
children.translated_text: And since in this way a producing activity is impossible in the three times, it does not exist.
For this very reason he says:
Activity is not possessed of conditions.
Thus.
There is no qualifier apart from the qualified thing.
This has been established in the <s>Madhyamakāvatāra</s> by words such as these.
For one does not say that the son of a barren woman possesses cows.
If so, then it will be without conditions, one might say.
That too is unreasonable, as he says:

children.text: pratyayavatī nāsti tadā kathamapratyayavatī nirhetukā syāt
children.translated_text: When it does not exist as possessed of conditions, how then could it be without conditions, that is, without a cause?
When, indeed?

children.text: na hi tantumayaḥ paṭo na yukta iti viraṇamayo 'bhyupagamyate ||
children.translated_text: For because a cloth made of threads is not reasonable, one does not accept a cloth made of reed-fibers.
Therefore activity does not produce an entity.
Here someone says:
If in this way activity is impossible,
then the conditions will be producers of entities.
Thus.
It is replied:

children.text: yadā kriyā nāsti tadā kriyārahitā akriyāvanto nirhetukāḥ pratyayāḥ kathaṃ janakāḥ ||
children.translated_text: When activity does not exist, how can conditions that are devoid of activity, inactive, and causeless be producers?
But perhaps only those that possess activity are producers.
It is replied:
The connection is with the preceding 'not.'
The word 'uta' has the sense of restriction.

children.text: tatra kriyāyā abhāva uktaḥ kathaṃ kriyāvattvaṃ pratyayānāmiti ||
children.translated_text: There the absence of activity has been stated; how, then, could conditions possess activity?
And just as an activity producing consciousness has been discussed,

children.text: evaṃ parikriyādayo'pi bhāvā uktā veditavyā iti nāsti kriyāto'pi samutpattirbhāvānāmiti bhavatyutpādābhidhānam arthaśūnyaṃ ||
children.translated_text: so too activities such as preparatory cooking should be understood as discussed. Thus there is no arising of entities even from activity, and the expression 'arising of an entity' is devoid of meaning.
Here someone says:

children.text: kiṃ na etena kriyāvattaḥ pratyayā ityādivicāreṇa ||
children.translated_text: What is the use of this investigation, beginning with 'conditions are possessed of activity'?

children.text: yasmāccakṣurādīn pratītya pratyayān vijñānādayo bhāvā jāyante ||
children.translated_text: For entities such as consciousness arise in dependence upon conditions such as the eye and the rest.
Therefore the eye and the rest have the status of conditions, and from them there is the arising of consciousness and the rest.
Saying that this too is not reasonable, he states:

children.text: tatra nāsmin parapratyayo'stītyaparapratyayaṃ paropadeśāgamyaṃ svayam evādhigantavyam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, 'it has no condition in another' means that it is not dependent on another, not accessible through another's teaching, and must be realized only by oneself.

children.text: yathā hi taimirikā vitathaṃ keśamaśakamakṣikādirūpaṃ paśyanto vitimiropadeśenāpi na śaknuvanti keśānāṃ yathāvad avasthitaṃ svarūpam adarśananyāyenādhigantavyam ataimirikā ivādhigantum ||
children.translated_text: For just as people with cataracts, seeing false forms such as hairs, gnats, and flies, cannot, even through the instruction of those free from cataracts, realize the actual nature of the hairs as it stands by way of non-seeing, as those without cataracts realize it,

children.text: kiṃ tarhy ataimirikopadeśān mithyaitad ityetāvanmātrakameva pratipadyante ||
children.translated_text: rather, from the instruction of those without cataracts they understand only this much: 'This is false.'

children.text: yadā tu timiropaghātyaviparītaśūnyatādarśanāñjanāñjitabuddhinayanāḥ santaḥ samutpannatattvajñānā bhavanti tadā tat tattvam anadhigamanayogena svayamadhigacchantīti ||
children.translated_text: But when, their eyes of understanding anointed with the collyrium of the vision of emptiness, the antidote to cataract, they have arisen into knowledge of reality, then, through the manner of not apprehending that thing, they realize that reality for themselves.
In this way, the own-nature of entities that is not dependent on another is their reality.
And this has a peaceful nature; that is, it is devoid of intrinsic nature, like the non-seeing of hairs by one without cataracts.
For this very reason it is not elaborated by elaborations.

children.text: prapañco hi vāk prapañcayatyarthān iti kṛtvā ||
children.translated_text: For elaboration is speech, since it elaborates meanings.
Thus 'not elaborated by elaborations' means not expressed by words.
And that is non-conceptual.
Conceptual construction is the activity of mind; because reality is free from that, it is non-conceptual.
As it is said in a sūtra:
What is ultimate truth?
Where even knowledge has no movement, what need is there to speak of syllables?
Thus it is non-conceptual.
'It has manifold meaning' means it has distinct meanings.
'It does not have manifold meaning' means it has non-distinct meaning, that is, undivided meaning.
As stated in the noble <s>Satyadvayāvatāra-sūtra</s>:
The <s>Devaputra</s> said, 'What, then, <s>Mañjuśrī</s>, is right application?'
<s>Mañjuśrī</s> said:

children.text: yatsamā devapūtra paramārthatas tathatā dharmadhātur atyantājātiśca tatsamāni paramārthataḥ pañcānantaryāṇi yatsamāni pañcānantaryāṇi tatsamāni dṛṣṭikṛtāni
children.translated_text: Just as, <s>Devaputra</s>, suchness, the <s>dharmadhātu</s> (realm of phenomena), and absolute non-birth are equal ultimately, so too the five immediate sins are equal ultimately; and just as the five immediate sins are equal, so too things produced by views are equal.
Just as things produced by views are equal, so too the dharmas of ordinary beings are equal.
Just as the dharmas of ordinary beings are equal, so too the dharmas of trainees are equal.
Just as the dharmas of trainees are equal, so too the dharmas of non-trainees are equal.
Just as the dharmas of non-trainees are equal, so too the dharmas of perfectly awakened Buddhas are equal.
Just as the dharmas of perfectly awakened Buddhas are equal, so too nirvāṇa is equal.
Just as nirvāṇa is equal, so too saṃsāra is equal.
Just as saṃsāra is equal, so too defilement is equal ultimately.
Just as defilement is equal ultimately, so too purification is equal ultimately.

children.text: yatsamaṃ paramārthato vyavadānaṃ tatsamāḥ paramārthataḥ sarvadharmāḥ
children.translated_text: Just as purification is equal ultimately, so too all dharmas are equal ultimately.

children.text: evaṃ paramārthataḥ sarvadharmasamatāprayukto devaputra bhikṣuḥ samyakprayukta ityucyate
children.translated_text: In this way, <s>Devaputra</s>, a monk who is applied to the equality of all dharmas ultimately is called rightly applied.
The <s>Devaputra</s> said:

children.text: katamayā punarmañjuśrīḥ samatayā yāvatparamārthato yatsamaṃ vyavadānaṃ tatsamāḥ sarvadharmāḥ paramārthata iti
children.translated_text: By what equality, then, <s>Mañjuśrī</s>, is it said up to: 'Just as purification is equal ultimately, so too all dharmas are equal ultimately'?
<s>Mañjuśrī</s> said:

children.text: paramārthataḥ sarvadharmānutpādasamatayā paramārthataḥ sarvadharmātyantājātisamatayā paramārthataḥ samāḥ sarvadharmāḥ
children.translated_text: By the equality of the non-arising of all dharmas ultimately, and by the equality of the absolute non-birth of all dharmas ultimately, all dharmas are equal ultimately.
For what reason?

children.text: paramārthato nirvāṇakaraṇā hi devaputra sarvadharmā atyantanirutpādatāmupādāya
children.translated_text: For ultimately, <s>Devaputra</s>, all dharmas are makers of nirvāṇa, on account of their absolute non-production.

children.text: tadyathāpi nāma devaputra yacca mṛdbhājanasyābhyantaram ākāśaṃ yacca ratnabhājanasyābhyantaram ākāśaṃ ākāśadhāturevaiṣaḥ
children.translated_text: For example, <s>Devaputra</s>, the space inside an earthen vessel and the space inside a jeweled vessel are just the element of space.
Ultimately there is no distinction at all in that.

children.text: evameva devaputra yaḥ saṃkleśaḥ sa paramārthato 'tyantānutpādatā
children.translated_text: In exactly the same way, <s>Devaputra</s>, whatever is defilement is ultimately absolute non-arising.
Whatever is purification is also ultimately absolute non-arising.
Saṃsāra too is ultimately absolute non-arising.
And so on, even nirvāṇa is ultimately absolute non-arising.
Here there is no distinction at all ultimately.
For what reason?
Because all dharmas are ultimately absolutely unproduced.
Therefore, in this way, non-manifoldness of meaning should be understood as the characteristic of reality, because it has the single taste of emptiness.
And here each subsequent explanation should be understood as explaining the previous one.
Thus, first, this is the characteristic of reality for the noble ones who have done what had to be done for the complete exhaustion of the saṃsāra of birth, old age, and death.
But with reference to the worldly characteristic of reality, it is said:
